ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: Quadrilateral DEFG is a rectangle. If $DF = 2(x + 5) - 7$ and $EG = 3(x - 2)$, find EG.
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The diagram shows quadrilateral DEFG as a rectangle, with D at the upper left, E at the upper right, F at the lower right, and G at the lower left. Both diagonals are drawn: DF connects D to F, and EG connects E to G. Reasoning: In a rectangle, the diagonals are congruent, so DF = EG. Given DF = 2(x + 5) - 7 and EG = 3(x - 2), set them equal: 2(x + 5) - 7 = 3(x - 2). Simplify: 2x + 10 - 7 = 3x - 6, so 2x + 3 = 3x - 6. Solving gives x = 9. Then EG = 3(x - 2) = 3(9 - 2) = 3(7) = 21.

method.method_draft: Read the image as showing a rectangle with right angles and opposite sides parallel; DF runs from D to F and EG runs from E to G. Instead of invoking the diagonal theorem directly, reason through right triangles: diagonal DF is the hypotenuse of right triangle DGF, with legs DG and GF; diagonal EG is the hypotenuse of right triangle EFG or EGD, with corresponding rectangle side lengths equal to DG and GF because opposite sides of a rectangle are equal. Thus both diagonals have length sqrt(DG^2 + GF^2), so DF = EG. Then use the text expressions to write 2(x + 5) - 7 = 3(x - 2), solve x = 9, and compute EG = 3(9 - 2) = 21.
